BUG: Chained urls (allowed by fsspec) not recognized by is_fsspec_url
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from pandas.io.common import is_fsspec_url
import fsspec

# This fsspec trick chains a cache fs with an s3 file system using "::".
# See https://filesystem-spec.readthedocs.io/en/latest/features.html#url-chaining.
fn = "filecache::s3://ncei-wcsd-archive/data/processed/SH1305/18kHz/SaKe2013-D20130523-T080854_to_SaKe2013-D20130523-T085643.csv"

with fsspec.open(fn, storage_options={"s3": {"anon": True}}) as f:
    foo = pd.read_csv(f)

print(foo.shape)

# But this url isn't recognized as a valid fsspec url by pandas...
print(pd.io.common.is_fsspec_url(fn))

# ...and so attempts to use chained url directly fail:
bar = pd.read_csv("filecache::s3://ncei-wcsd-archive/data/processed/SH1305/18kHz/"
                 "SaKe2013-D20130523-T080854_to_SaKe2013-D20130523-T085643.csv",
                 storage_options={"s3": {"anon": True},
                                  "filecache":{"cache_storage":"/tmp/cache"}})
```


### Issue Description

fsspec allows one to pass "chained" urls (useful, e.g., for caching), for example "filecache::https://example.com/my_file".  However, since commit eeff2b0c3b meant to address issue #36271 supplying urls of this form to e.g., pd.read_csv has failed.

### Expected Behavior

Pandas should pass the chained url to fsspec.  In the example code, pd.Dataframes foo and bar should be identical.

        "http://example.com/file.csv",  # Regular HTTP
        "https://example.com/file.csv",  # Regular HTTPS
        "file:///local/path/file.txt",  # Regular file (not chained)
        "not-a-url",
        "filecache::http://example.com/file.csv",  # Chained with HTTP
        "filecache::https://example.com/file.csv",  # Chained with HTTPS
        "filecache::",  # Empty after ::
        "::s3://bucket/path",  # Empty before ::
        "filecache::invalid-url-without-protocol",
    ]
    
    # Test cases with multiple :: separators
    multiple_separators = [
        "cache1::cache2::s3://bucket/path",  # Should check cache2::s3://...
        "a::b::c::d::s3://bucket/path",  # Should check c::d::s3://...
    ]
    
    print("Testing valid chained URLs...")
    for url in valid_cases:
        result = is_fsspec_url(url)
        expected = not url.startswith(("filecache::http", "filecache::https"))
        status = "✅" if result == expected else "❌"
        print(f"{status} {url}: {result} (expected: {expected})")
    
    print("\nTesting invalid URLs...")
    for url in invalid_cases:

        status = "✅" if result == expected else "❌"
        print(f"{status} {url}: {result} (expected: {expected})")
    
    print("\nTesting multiple :: separators...")

        # Should check the part after the first ::
        chained_part = url.split("::", 1)[1]
        expected = bool(chained_part.startswith("s3://"))
        status = "✅" if result == expected else "❌"
        print(f"{status} {url}: {result} (expected: {expected})")

if __name__ == "__main__":

        local_file = f.name

        is_fsspec = pd.io.common.is_fsspec_url(chained_file_url)
        print(f"Test 2 - Chained file URL recognition: {is_fsspec}")
        
        # Note: We don't actually test reading with chained file:// because
        # fsspec might not handle local file caching in the same way
        
    finally:
        os.unlink(local_file)
    
    # Test 3: Test with BytesIO (non-fsspec path)
    buffer = io.StringIO(test_data)
    df3 = pd.read_csv(buffer)
    print(f"Test 3 - StringIO reading: {df3.shape}")

    test_urls = [

        result = pd.io.common.is_fsspec_url(url)

    assert is_fsspec_url("file:///local/path/file.txt")
    
    # Test malformed chained URLs
    assert not is_fsspec_url("filecache::")
    assert not is_fsspec_url("::s3://bucket/path")
    assert not is_fsspec_url("filecache::invalid-url")

The fix involves adding explicit handling for CategoricalDtype in the convert_dtypes function to preserve the categorical nature of the data, even when dtype_backend='pyarrow' is specified. The key insight is that categorical dtypes should not be converted to pyarrow-backed types when they are empty, as this breaks the expected behavior and causes the ArrowNotImplementedError for null types.
```python
import pandas as pd
ser = pd.Series(True, index=range(10_000_000), dtype='boolean')
```

### Issue Description

The behavior of the `.isin()` function on nullable boolean `boolean` series is inconsistent for `pd.NA`:  
For short series, this returns a series with `True` for every null values in the original series

```python
1    False
2     True
```

"""
Reproduce the issue described in the GitHub issue:
BUG: boolean series .isin([pd.NA]) inconsistent for series length
"""

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def test_short_series():
    """Test isin with short series - should work"""
    print("Testing short series...")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, pd.NA], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([pd.NA])
    print(f"Short series result: {result}")
    print(f"Expected: [False, False, True]")
    print(f"Sum of True values: {result.sum()}")
    assert result.sum() == 1, f"Expected 1 True value, got {result.sum()}"
    print("✓ Short series test passed\n")

def test_long_series():
    """Test isin with long series - should work consistently"""
    print("Testing long series...")
    ser = pd.Series(True, index=range(1_000_001), dtype='boolean')
    ser.iloc[0] = pd.NA
    ser.iloc[1] = False
    
    try:
        result = ser.isin([False, pd.NA])
        print(f"Long series result length: {len(result)}")
        print(f"Sum of True values: {result.sum()}")
        assert result.sum() == 2, f"Expected 2 True values, got {result.sum()}"
        print("✓ Long series test passed")
    except TypeError as e:
        print(f"✗ Long series test failed with TypeError: {e}")
        return False
    
    return True

def test_boundary_cases():
    """Test boundary cases around the threshold"""
    print("Testing boundary cases...")
    
    # Test just below threshold
    ser_1m = pd.Series(True, index=range(1_000_000), dtype='boolean')
    ser_1m.iloc[0] = pd.NA
    result_1m = ser_1m.isin([pd.NA])
    print(f"1M series: {len(result_1m)} elements, {result_1m.sum()} True values")
    
    # Test just above threshold
    ser_1m_1 = pd.Series(True, index=range(1_000_001), dtype='boolean')
    ser_1m_1.iloc[0] = pd.NA
    try:
        result_1m_1 = ser_1m_1.isin([pd.NA])
        print(f"1M+1 series: {len(result_1m_1)} elements, {result_1m_1.sum()} True values")
        print("✓ Boundary cases passed")
        return True
    except TypeError as e:
        print(f"✗ Boundary cases failed with TypeError: {e}")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Reproducing the issue described in GitHub issue...")
    print("=" * 50)
    
    test_short_series()
    
    success = test_long_series()
    if not success:
        print("Issue reproduced: TypeError for long series")
    
    test_boundary_cases()
    
    print("\nReproduction complete.")</parameter>

"""
Additional edge case tests for the boolean series .isin([pd.NA]) fix
"""

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def test_boolean_isin_with_na_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases for boolean series isin with pd.NA"""
    
    print("Testing edge cases for boolean series isin with pd.NA...")
    
    # Test 1: Very long series with pd.NA at different positions
    print("\n1. Very long series with pd.NA at different positions")
    ser = pd.Series(True, index=range(2_000_000), dtype='boolean')
    ser.iloc[0] = pd.NA
    ser.iloc[1_000_000] = pd.NA
    ser.iloc[1_999_999] = False
    result = ser.isin([False, pd.NA])
    assert result.sum() == 3, f"Expected 3 True values, got {result.sum()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 2: Series with all possible boolean values and NA
    print("\n2. Series with all possible boolean values and NA")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, pd.NA, True, False, pd.NA], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([pd.NA])
    expected = [False, False, True, False, False, True]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result.tolist()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 3: Empty values list
    print("\n3. Empty values list")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, pd.NA], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([])
    assert result.sum() == 0, f"Expected 0 True values, got {result.sum()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 4: Values with only pd.NA
    print("\n4. Values with only pd.NA")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, pd.NA], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([pd.NA])
    expected = [False, False, True]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result.tolist()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 5: Mixed types in values (should still work)
    print("\n5. Mixed types in values")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, pd.NA], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([True, pd.NA, 42])  # 42 should be ignored
    expected = [True, False, True]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result.tolist()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 6: Large series with boundary length
    print("\n6. Large series with boundary length")
    for length in [999_999, 1_000_000, 1_000_001, 1_000_002]:
        ser = pd.Series(True, index=range(length), dtype='boolean')
        ser.iloc[0] = pd.NA
        result = ser.isin([pd.NA])
        assert result.sum() == 1, f"Length {length}: Expected 1 True value, got {result.sum()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 7: Series with NaN (not pd.NA)
    print("\n7. Series with NaN (not pd.NA)")
    ser = pd.Series([True, False, np.nan], dtype='boolean')
    result = ser.isin([np.nan])
    expected = [False, False, True]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, f"Expected {expected}, got {result.tolist()}"
    print("✓ Passed")
    
    # Test 8: Performance test with very large series
    print("\n8. Performance test with very large series")
    import time
    ser = pd.Series(True, index=range(5_000_000), dtype='boolean')
    ser.iloc[0] = pd.NA
    ser.iloc[1_000_000] = False
    ser.iloc[2_000_000] = pd.NA
    ser.iloc[3_000_000] = False
    
    start_time = time.time()
    result = ser.isin([False, pd.NA])
    end_time = time.time()
    
    assert result.sum() == 4, f"Expected 4 True values, got {result.sum()}"
    print(f"✓ Passed - Completed in {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")
    
    print("\nAll edge case tests passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_boolean_isin_with_na_edge_cases()</parameter>

        print(f"  ✗ __getitem__ failed: {e}")
        return False

"""
Edge case tests for the new dict support in pd.set_option
"""

import pandas as pd
import pytest

def test_dict_empty():
    """Test empty dict"""
    pd.set_option({})
    # Should not raise any errors

def test_dict_single_option():
    """Test dict with single option"""
    pd.set_option({'display.precision': 5})
    assert pd.get_option('display.precision') == 5

def test_dict_multiple_options():
    """Test dict with multiple options"""
    original_precision = pd.get_option('display.precision')
    original_max_col = pd.get_option('display.max_columns')
    
    pd.set_option({
        'display.precision': 3,
        'display.max_columns': 50,
        'styler.format.precision': 1
    })
    
    assert pd.get_option('display.precision') == 3
    assert pd.get_option('display.max_columns') == 50
    assert pd.get_option('styler.format.precision') == 1
    
    # Reset to original values
    pd.set_option('display.precision', original_precision)
    pd.set_option('display.max_columns', original_max_col)

def test_dict_invalid_option():
    """Test dict with invalid option"""
    with pytest.raises(Exception):  # Should raise OptionError
        pd.set_option({'invalid.option': 'value'})

def test_mixed_args_and_kwargs():
    """Test mixing args and kwargs (should prioritize kwargs)"""
    original_precision = pd.get_option('display.precision')
    
    # This should use kwargs and ignore args
    pd.set_option({'display.precision': 7}, display__precision=8)
    assert pd.get_option('display.precision') == 8
    
    pd.set_option('display.precision', original_precision)

def test_kwargs_format():
    """Test kwargs with double underscore format"""
    original_precision = pd.get_option('display.precision')
    
    pd.set_option(display__precision=9)
    assert pd.get_option('display.precision') == 9
    
    pd.set_option('display.precision', original_precision)

def test_nested_option_dict():
    """Test nested options via dict"""
    original_max_col = pd.get_option('display.max_columns')
    
    pd.set_option({
        'display.max_columns': 75,
        'mode.chained_assignment': 'warn'
    })
    
    assert pd.get_option('display.max_columns') == 75
    
    pd.set_option('display.max_columns', original_max_col)

def test_dict_with_none_values():
    """Test dict with None values"""
    original_max_col = pd.get_option('display.max_columns')
    
    pd.set_option({'display.max_columns': None})
    # None should be treated as a valid value
    
    pd.set_option('display.max_columns', original_max_col)

def test_large_dict():
    """Test large dictionary with many options"""
    original_values = {}
    options_to_test = [
        'display.precision',
        'display.max_columns',
        'display.max_rows',
        'display.width',
        'styler.format.precision'
    ]
    
    # Store original values
    for opt in options_to_test:
        original_values[opt] = pd.get_option(opt)
    
    # Create large dict
    large_dict = {
        opt: idx + 1 for idx, opt in enumerate(options_to_test)
    }
    
    pd.set_option(large_dict)
    
    # Verify all values were set
    for opt, expected in large_dict.items():
        assert pd.get_option(opt) == expected
    
    # Reset to original values
    for opt, value in original_values.items():
        pd.set_option(opt, value)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_dict_empty()
    test_dict_single_option()
    test_dict_multiple_options()
    test_dict_invalid_option()
    test_mixed_args_and_kwargs()
    test_kwargs_format()
    test_nested_option_dict()
    test_dict_with_none_values()
    test_large_dict()
    print("All edge case tests passed!")</parameter>
</function>

import pandas as pd

def test_edge_cases():
    """Test various edge cases for integer column names."""

    df1 = pd.DataFrame({1: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]})

    df2 = pd.DataFrame({1: [1, 2, 3], 2: [4, 5, 6], 3: [7, 8, 9]})
    result2 = df2.query("`1` > 1 and `2` < 6")
    print(f"df2.query('`1` > 1 and `2` < 6'): {len(result2)} rows")
    assert len(result2) == 1
    
    # Test 3: Mixed integer and string columns
    print("\n3. Mixed integer and string columns:")
    df3 = pd.DataFrame({1: [1, 2, 3], 'a': [4, 5, 6], 2: [7, 8, 9]})
    result3 = df3.query("`1` > 1 and `a` > 4")
    print(f"df3.query('`1` > 1 and `a` > 4'): {len(result3)} rows")
    assert len(result3) == 2
    
    # Test 4: Negative integer column
    print("\n4. Negative integer column:")
    df4 = pd.DataFrame({-1: [1, 2, 3]})
    result4 = df4.query("`-1` > 1")
    print(f"df4.query('`-1` > 1'): {len(result4)} rows")
    assert len(result4) == 2
    
    # Test 5: Zero as column name
    print("\n5. Zero as column name:")
    df5 = pd.DataFrame({0: [1, 2, 3]})
    result5 = df5.query("`0` == 2")
    print(f"df5.query('`0` == 2'): {len(result5)} rows")
    assert len(result5) == 1
    
    # Test 6: Large integer column
    print("\n6. Large integer column:")
    df6 = pd.DataFrame({999999: [1, 2, 3]})
    result6 = df6.query("`999999` > 1")
    print(f"df6.query('`999999` > 1'): {len(result6)} rows")
    assert len(result6) == 2
    
    # Test 7: Float column name (edge case)
    print("\n7. Float column name:")
    df7 = pd.DataFrame({1.5: [1, 2, 3]})
    result7 = df7.query("`1.5` > 1")
    print(f"df7.query('`1.5` > 1'): {len(result7)} rows")
    assert len(result7) == 3
    
    # Test 8: Ensure string columns still work
    print("\n8. String columns still work:")
    df8 = pd.DataFrame({'col 1': [1, 2, 3], 'col-2': [4, 5, 6]})
    result8 = df8.query("`col 1` > 1 and `col-2` > 4")
    print(f"df8.query('`col 1` > 1 and `col-2` > 4'): {len(result8)} rows")
    assert len(result8) == 2
    
    # Test 9: Ensure existing functionality with special characters
    print("\n9. Special characters in column names:")
    df9 = pd.DataFrame({'col with spaces': [1, 2, 3], 'col-with-dashes': [4, 5, 6]})
    result9 = df9.query("`col with spaces` > 1")
    print(f"df9.query('`col with spaces` > 1'): {len(result9)} rows")
    assert len(result9) == 2
    
    print("\n=== All Edge Cases Passed! ===")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_edge_cases()</parameter>


### Issue Description

Also effects other Series methods called on the result of a binary operation, which work well if applied to one operand.

See also https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/24670

### Expected Behavior

Should return a Series of sums with nan values removed. Generally I would expect that it should be possible to apply a Series method to the result of a binary operation as part of an eval expression.

import numpy as np

def test_issue():
    """Test the issue described in the GitHub issue"""
    print("Testing empty DataFrame resampling issue...")
    
    # Create empty DataFrame with DatetimeIndex
    df = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.DatetimeIndex([]))
    print(f"Original index type: {type(df.index)}")
    print(f"Original index: {df.index}")
    
    # Test resampling with ffill (upsampling)
    resampled = df.resample("D").ffill()
    print(f"Resampled index type: {type(resampled.index)}")
    print(f"Resampled index: {resampled.index}")
    
    # Verify issue exists
    assert isinstance(df.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), "Original should be DatetimeIndex"
    
    # This should fail with the bug - it should be DatetimeIndex but becomes MultiIndex
    try:
        assert isinstance(resampled.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), "Resampled should be DatetimeIndex"
        print("✅ ISSUE FIXED: Resampled index is DatetimeIndex")
    except AssertionError:
        print("❌ ISSUE EXISTS: Resampled index is NOT DatetimeIndex")
        print(f"   Actual type: {type(resampled.index)}")
        return False
    
    return True

def test_other_methods():
    """Test other upsampling methods mentioned in the issue"""
    print("\nTesting other upsampling methods...")
    
    methods = ['fillna', 'ffill', 'bfill', 'nearest', 'asfreq', 'interpolate']
    
    for method in methods:
        try:
            df = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.DatetimeIndex([]))
            
            if method == 'fillna':
                result = df.resample("D").fillna(method='ffill')
            elif method == 'interpolate':
                # interpolate needs at least one non-empty column
                df['value'] = []
                result = df.resample("D").interpolate()
            elif method == 'asfreq':
                result = df.resample("D").asfreq()
            else:
                result = getattr(df.resample("D"), method)()
            
            print(f"Method {method}: index type = {type(result.index)}")
            if not isinstance(result.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
                print(f"  ❌ {method} failed - got {type(result.index)}")
                return False
            else:
                print(f"  ✅ {method} works correctly")
                
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  ❌ {method} failed with exception: {e}")
            return False
    
    return True

def test_non_empty():
    """Test that non-empty dataframes still work correctly"""
    print("\nTesting non-empty DataFrame for regression...")
    
    dates = pd.date_range('2023-01-01', periods=3, freq='D')
    df = pd.DataFrame({'value': [1, 2, 3]}, index=dates)
    
    resampled = df.resample("6H").ffill()
    print(f"Non-empty DataFrame resampled index type: {type(resampled.index)}")
    
    assert isinstance(resampled.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), "Non-empty should still work"
    print("✅ Non-empty DataFrame works correctly")
    return True

def test_downsampling():
    """Test that downsampling still works correctly"""
    print("\nTesting downsampling for regression...")
    
    dates = pd.date_range('2023-01-01', periods=10, freq='D')
    df = pd.DataFrame({'value': range(10)}, index=dates)
    
    resampled = df.resample("W").mean()
    print(f"Downsampling DataFrame resampled index type: {type(resampled.index)}")
    
    assert isinstance(resampled.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), "Downsampling should still work"
    print("✅ Downsampling works correctly")
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = True
    success &= test_issue()
    success &= test_other_methods()
    success &= test_non_empty()
    success &= test_downsampling()
    
    if success:
        print("\n🎉 All tests passed!")
    else:
        print("\n💥 Some tests failed!")</parameter>

    print("\n1. Empty DataFrame with named DatetimeIndex")

    result = df.resample("D").ffill()
    print(f"Timezone preserved: {result.index.tz}")
    assert result.index.tz is not None, "Timezone should be preserved"

- Added a conditional check to only align timezones when they are actually different

   831         using nested LaTeX commands with their accompanied options.

   834

   836         >>> s = df.style.highlight_max(axis=None,

   843         ...                            props='cellcolor:{red}; bfseries: ;')
   844         >>> s.to_latex()  # doctest: +SKIP

   846         Internally these structured LaTeX ``(<command>, <options>)`` pairs
   847         are translated to the
   848         ``display_value`` with the default structure:
   849         ``\<command><options> <display_value>``.

def test_edge_cases():

            expected = df1[df1['col'] == 'single']
            print(f"Single category test: {len(result) == len(expected) and result.equals(expected)}")

        print("\nTest 2: Empty categories")
        cat2 = pd.api.types.CategoricalDtype(categories=[])

        with pd.HDFStore(h5_file, 'w') as store:
            store.append('df2', df2, data_columns=['col'])
        
        with pd.HDFStore(h5_file, 'r') as store:

            expected = df2[df2['col'] == 'missing']
            print(f"Empty categories test: {len(result) == len(expected) and result.equals(expected)}")

        print("\nTest 3: Numeric categories")
        cat3 = pd.api.types.CategoricalDtype(categories=[1, 2, 3])
        df3 = pd.DataFrame({'col': [1, 2, 3], 'val': [10, 20, 30]}).astype({'col': cat3, 'val': int})

            store.append('df3', df3, data_columns=['col'])
        
        with pd.HDFStore(h5_file, 'r') as store:

            expected = df3[df3['col'] == 2]
            print(f"Numeric categories test: {len(result) == len(expected) and result.equals(expected)}")
        
        # Test case 4: Mixed case categories

        cat4 = pd.api.types.CategoricalDtype(categories=['A', 'b', 'C'])
        df4 = pd.DataFrame({'col': ['A', 'b', 'C'], 'val': [1, 2, 3]}).astype({'col': cat4, 'val': int})

        cat5 = pd.api.types.CategoricalDtype(categories=large_categories)
        df5 = pd.DataFrame({

        print("\nAll edge case tests completed!")
        
    finally:
        if os.path.exists(h5_file):
            os.remove(h5_file)

if __name__ == "__main__":

In particular, `map` will use `NaN` when the mapping returns `None`, but it will use `None` when the function returns `None`. Also, if we stop supporting dictionaries, users in general should just replace their code from `Series.map(my_dict)` to `Series.map(my_dict.get)`. But there are some special cases, for example when the dictionary is a `defaultdict`, `.get` will return `None`, while the current `map` implementation with a `defaultdict` will consider the default value.

        """
        Map values of Series according to an input mapping or function.

        Used for substituting each value in a Series with another value,
        that may be derived from a function, a ``dict`` or
        a :class:`Series`.

        Parameters
        ----------
        arg : function, collections.abc.Mapping subclass or Series
            Mapping correspondence.
        na_action : {None, 'ignore'}, default None
            If 'ignore', propagate NaN values, without passing them to the
            mapping correspondence.
        **kwargs
            Additional keyword arguments to pass as keywords arguments to
            `arg`.

            .. versionadded:: 3.0.0

        Returns
        -------
        Series
            Same index as caller.

        See Also
        --------
        Series.apply : For applying more complex functions on a Series.
        Series.replace: Replace values given in `to_replace` with `value`.
        DataFrame.apply : Apply a function row-/column-wise.
        DataFrame.map : Apply a function elementwise on a whole DataFrame.

        Notes
        -----
        When ``arg`` is a dictionary, values in Series that are not in the
        dictionary (as keys) are converted to ``NaN``. However, if the
        dictionary is a ``dict`` subclass that defines ``__missing__`` (i.e.
        provides a method for default values), then this default is used
        rather than ``NaN``.

        Examples
        --------
        >>> s = pd.Series(["cat", "dog", np.nan, "rabbit"])
        >>> s
        0      cat
        1      dog
        2      NaN
        3   rabbit
        dtype: object

        ``map`` accepts a ``dict`` or a ``Series``. Values that are not found
        in the ``dict`` are converted to ``NaN``, unless the dict has a default
        value (e.g. ``defaultdict``):

        >>> s.map({"cat": "kitten", "dog": "puppy"})
        0   kitten
        1    puppy
        2      NaN
        3      NaN
        dtype: object

        It also accepts a function:

        >>> s.map("I am a {}".format)
        0       I am a cat
        1       I am a dog
        2       I am a nan
        3    I am a rabbit
        dtype: object

        To avoid applying the function to missing values (and keep them as
        ``NaN``) ``na_action='ignore'`` can be used:

        >>> s.map("I am a {}".format, na_action="ignore")
        0     I am a cat
        1     I am a dog
        2            NaN
        3  I am a rabbit
        dtype: object
        """

            arg = functools.partial(arg, **kwargs)
        new_values = self._map_values(arg, na_action=na_action)

"""
Edge case tests for Series.map parameter rename from 'arg' to 'func'
"""

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict
import warnings

def test_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases for Series.map parameter rename"""
    
    print("Testing edge cases...")
    
    # Test 1: Backward compatibility - positional arguments
    s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    result = s.map(lambda x: x * 2)
    assert result.tolist() == [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], "Backward compatibility failed"
    print("✓ Backward compatibility with positional args")
    
    # Test 2: New parameter name 'func' works
    result = s.map(func=lambda x: x * 3)
    assert result.tolist() == [3, 6, 9, 12, 15], "New parameter name failed"
    print("✓ New parameter name 'func' works")
    
    # Test 3: Dict mapping with new parameter
    mapping = {1: 'a', 2: 'b', 3: 'c'}
    result = s.map(func=mapping)
    expected = ['a', 'b', 'c', np.nan, np.nan]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, "Dict mapping with new param failed"
    print("✓ Dict mapping with new parameter name")
    
    # Test 4: Series mapping with new parameter
    mapping_series = pd.Series(['x', 'y', 'z'], index=[1, 2, 3])
    result = s.map(func=mapping_series)
    expected = ['x', 'y', 'z', np.nan, np.nan]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, "Series mapping with new param failed"
    print("✓ Series mapping with new parameter name")
    
    # Test 5: defaultdict behavior
    default_dict = defaultdict(lambda: 'default')
    default_dict.update({1: 'one', 2: 'two'})
    result = s.map(func=default_dict)
    expected = ['one', 'two', 'default', 'default', 'default']
    assert result.tolist() == expected, "defaultdict mapping failed"
    print("✓ defaultdict mapping works")
    
    # Test 6: kwargs forwarding
    def multiply(x, factor=1):
        return x * factor
    
    result = s.map(func=multiply, factor=10)
    assert result.tolist() == [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], "kwargs forwarding failed"
    print("✓ kwargs forwarding works")
    
    # Test 7: na_action parameter still works
    s_with_nan = pd.Series([1, 2, np.nan, 4])
    result = s_with_nan.map(func=lambda x: x * 2, na_action='ignore')
    expected = [2.0, 4.0, np.nan, 8.0]
    assert result.tolist() == expected, "na_action parameter failed"
    print("✓ na_action parameter works")
    
    # Test 8: Complex callable with new parameter
    class CustomMapper:
        def __call__(self, x):
            return f"value_{x}"
    
    mapper = CustomMapper()
    result = s.map(func=mapper)
    expected = ['value_1', 'value_2', 'value_3', 'value_4', 'value_5']
    assert result.tolist() == expected, "Complex callable failed"
    print("✓ Complex callable works")
    
    print("All edge case tests passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_edge_cases()</parameter>

"""
Reproduction script for the issue described in the GitHub issue:
BUG: df.plot() "Subplots" changes behavior of how values are stacked using the "Stacked" property
"""

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')  # Use non-interactive backend
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def test_stacked_behavior():
    """Test the stacked behavior with and without subplots"""
    
    # Create test data
    df = pd.DataFrame([(30, 10, 10), (20, 20, 20), (10, 30, 30)], columns=list('ABC'))
    
    print("Original DataFrame:")
    print(df)
    print()
    
    # Test 1: Normal stacked bar plot without subplots
    fig1, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    df.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=ax1)
    ax1.set_title("Without subplots - should stack properly")
    
    # Calculate expected stacked values for verification
    expected_stacked = df.sum(axis=1)
    print("Expected stacked values (A+B+C):", expected_stacked.tolist())
    
    # Test 2: Stacked bar plot with subplots - this is where the bug occurs
    fig2, axes = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 6))
    # Using subplots parameter with a tuple
    df.plot(subplots=[('A', 'B')], kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=axes)
    axes.set_title("With subplots - should also stack properly")
    
    # Save plots for visual inspection
    fig1.savefig('/testbed/test_without_subplots.png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    fig2.savefig('/testbed/test_with_subplots.png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    
    print("Plots saved to /testbed/test_without_subplots.png and /testbed/test_with_subplots.png")
    
    # Let's also test the actual values being plotted
    # We need to examine the bar heights programmatically
    
    # For the first plot (without subplots)
    bars1 = ax1.containers
    if bars1:
        heights1 = []
        for container in bars1:
            heights1.append([rect.get_height() for rect in container])
        print("Heights without subplots:", heights1)
    
    # For the second plot (with subplots)
    bars2 = axes.containers
    if bars2:
        heights2 = []
        for container in bars2:
            heights2.append([rect.get_height() for rect in container])
        print("Heights with subplots:", heights2)
    
    plt.close('all')
    
    return df

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_stacked_behavior()</parameter>

    print("=== Test 1: Without subplots ===")
    bars1 = ax1.containers

    bars2 = axes.containers
    if bars2:
        for i, container in enumerate(bars2):
            heights = [rect.get_height() for rect in container]
            y_positions = [rect.get_y() for rect in container]
            print(f"Container {i} heights: {heights}")
            print(f"Container {i} y positions: {y_positions}")
            print(f"Container {i} sum of heights: {[h+p for h, p in zip(heights, y_positions)]}")
    
    # Save plots for visual inspection

    fig2.savefig('/testbed/detailed_with_subplots.png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    
    plt.close('all')
    
    # Test expected behavior: A+B should equal [40, 40, 40]
    expected = [40, 40, 40]  # A+B = [30+10, 20+20, 10+30]
    print(f"\nExpected A+B values: {expected}")
    
    return df

    # Test 2: Stacked bar plot with subplots - should now work correctly
    fig2, axes = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 6))
    # Using subplots parameter with a tuple
    df.plot(subplots=[('A', 'B')], kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=axes)
    
    # Test 3: Multiple subplots with stacking
    fig3, axes_list = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))
    df.plot(subplots=[('A', 'B'), ('C',)], kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=axes_list)

    else:

    print("\nPlots saved for visual inspection")

    print(f"\nExpected A+B values: {expected_ab}")
    print(f"Expected C values: {expected_c}")
    
    plt.close('all')
    
    return df

BUG: dot on Arrow Series produces a Numpy object result
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

series_result = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64")
)
series_result.dtype  # is dtype('O')

series_result_2 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float[pyarrow]").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float[pyarrow]")
)
series_result_2.dtype  # same, is dtype('O')

# `DataFrame.dot` was already fixed
df_result = pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64").T.dot(
    pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64")
)
df_result.dtype  # is Float64Dtype()
```

### Issue Description

`Series.dot` with Arrow or nullable dtypes returns series result with numpy object dtype. This was reported in #53979 and fixed for DataFrames in #54025.

Possibly side notes: I believe the "real" issue here is that the implementation uses `.values` which returns a `dtype=object` array for the DataFrame. This seems directly related to #60038 and at least somewhat related to #60301 (which is also referenced in a comment on the former).

### Expected Behavior

I would expect `Series.dot` to return the "best" common datatype for the input datatypes (in the examples, would expect the appropriate float dtype)

```python
import pandas as pd

series_result = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64")
)
series_result.dtype  # would expect Float64Dtype()

series_result_2 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float[pyarrow]").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float[pyarrow]")
)
series_result_2.dtype  # would expect float[pyarrow]
```

BUG: dot on Arrow Series produces a Numpy object result
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

series_result = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64")
)
series_result.dtype  # is dtype('O')

series_result_2 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float[pyarrow]").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float[pyarrow]")
)
series_result_2.dtype  # same, is dtype('O')

# `DataFrame.dot` was already fixed
df_result = pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64").T.dot(
    pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64")
)
df_result.dtype  # is Float64Dtype()
```

### Issue Description

`Series.dot` with Arrow or nullable dtypes returns series result with numpy object dtype. This was reported in #53979 and fixed for DataFrames in #54025.

Possibly side notes: I believe the "real" issue here is that the implementation uses `.values` which returns a `dtype=object` array for the DataFrame. This seems directly related to #60038 and at least somewhat related to #60301 (which is also referenced in a comment on the former).

### Expected Behavior

I would expect `Series.dot` to return the "best" common datatype for the input datatypes (in the examples, would expect the appropriate float dtype)

```python
import pandas as pd

series_result = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64")
)
series_result.dtype  # would expect Float64Dtype()

series_result_2 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float[pyarrow]").dot(
    pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float[pyarrow]")
)
series_result_2.dtype  # would expect float[pyarrow]
```

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def test_reproduce_issue():
    """Reproduce the issue described in the GitHub issue."""
    print("Testing Series.dot with nullable and Arrow dtypes...")
    
    # Test case 1: Float64 dtype
    print("\n1. Testing Float64 dtype:")
    series_result = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
        pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64")
    )
    print(f"   Result dtype: {series_result.dtype}")
    print(f"   Expected: Float64Dtype(), Got: {type(series_result.dtype)}")
    print(f"   Is object dtype: {series_result.dtype == np.dtype('O')}")
    
    # Test case 2: Arrow float dtype
    print("\n2. Testing float[pyarrow] dtype:")
    series_result_2 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float[pyarrow]").dot(
        pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float[pyarrow]")
    )
    print(f"   Result dtype: {series_result_2.dtype}")
    print(f"   Expected: float[pyarrow], Got: {type(series_result_2.dtype)}")
    print(f"   Is object dtype: {series_result_2.dtype == np.dtype('O')}")
    
    # Test case 3: Verify DataFrame.dot works correctly (as mentioned in issue)
    print("\n3. Testing DataFrame.dot (should work correctly):")
    df_result = pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="Float64").T.dot(
        pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64")
    )
    print(f"   Result dtype: {df_result.dtype}")
    print(f"   Expected: Float64Dtype(), Got: {type(df_result.dtype)}")
    print(f"   Is correct: {str(df_result.dtype) == 'Float64'}")

    # Test case 4: Regular numpy dtypes should still work
    print("\n4. Testing regular numpy float64:")
    series_result_3 = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="float64").dot(
        pd.DataFrame({"col1": {"a": 2.0}, "col2": {"a": 3.0}}, dtype="float64")
    )
    print(f"   Result dtype: {series_result_3.dtype}")
    print(f"   Expected: float64, Got: {type(series_result_3.dtype)}")
    
    # Test case 5: Test with Series dot Series
    print("\n5. Testing Series.dot(Series):")
    series_dot_series = pd.Series({"a": 1.0}, dtype="Float64").dot(
        pd.Series({"a": 2.0}, dtype="Float64")
    )
    print(f"   Result type: {type(series_dot_series)}")
    print(f"   Result value: {series_dot_series}")
    
    return {
        "float64_object_issue": series_result.dtype == np.dtype('O'),
        "arrow_object_issue": series_result_2.dtype == np.dtype('O'),
        "dataframe_works": str(df_result.dtype) == 'Float64',
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = test_reproduce_issue()
    print("\n" + "="*50)
    print("SUMMARY:")
    print(f"Float64 object dtype issue: {results['float64_object_issue']}")
    print(f"Arrow object dtype issue: {results['arrow_object_issue']}")
    print(f"DataFrame.dot works correctly: {results['dataframe_works']}")
    
    if results['float64_object_issue'] or results['arrow_object_issue']:
        print("\nISSUE CONFIRMED: Series.dot returns object dtype for nullable/Arrow dtypes")
    else:
        print("\nISSUE RESOLVED: Series.dot returns appropriate dtypes")</parameter>

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import pytest

def test_series_dot_nullable_dtypes():
    """Test Series.dot with nullable extension dtypes."""
    
    # Test Float64 dtype
    s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype="Float64")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="Float64")
    result = s.dot(df)
    expected_dtype = "Float64"
    assert str(result.dtype) == expected_dtype
    
    # Test Int64 dtype
    s_int = pd.Series([1, 2], dtype="Int64")
    df_int = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], dtype="Int64")
    result_int = s_int.dot(df_int)
    expected_int_dtype = "Int64"
    assert str(result_int.dtype) == expected_int_dtype
    
    # Test boolean dtype
    s_bool = pd.Series([True, False], dtype="boolean")
    df_bool = pd.DataFrame([[True, False], [False, True]], dtype="boolean")
    result_bool = s_bool.dot(df_bool)
    expected_bool_dtype = "Int64"  # boolean dot should promote to Int64
    assert str(result_bool.dtype) == expected_bool_dtype

def test_series_dot_arrow_dtypes():
    """Test Series.dot with Arrow extension dtypes."""
    
    # Test float[pyarrow] dtype
    s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype="float[pyarrow]")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="float[pyarrow]")
    result = s.dot(df)
    expected_dtype = "float[pyarrow]"
    assert str(result.dtype) == expected_dtype
    
    # Test int64[pyarrow] dtype
    s_int = pd.Series([1, 2], dtype="int64[pyarrow]")
    df_int = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], dtype="int64[pyarrow]")
    result_int = s_int.dot(df_int)
    expected_int_dtype = "int64[pyarrow]"
    assert str(result_int.dtype) == expected_int_dtype
    
    # Test string[pyarrow] dtype (should raise or handle gracefully)
    s_str = pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="string[pyarrow]")
    df_str = pd.DataFrame([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]], dtype="string[pyarrow]")
    try:
        result_str = s_str.dot(df_str)
        # This might not make sense for string dtypes
        print(f"String dot result: {result_str}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"String dot expected error: {e}")

def test_series_dot_mixed_dtypes():
    """Test Series.dot with mixed dtypes."""
    
    # Float64 with float64
    s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype="Float64")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="float64")
    result = s.dot(df)
    expected_dtype = "Float64"  # Should use the nullable extension dtype
    assert str(result.dtype) == expected_dtype
    
    # float64 with Float64
    s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype="float64")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="Float64")
    result = s.dot(df)
    expected_dtype = "Float64"  # Should use the nullable extension dtype
    assert str(result.dtype) == expected_dtype
    
    # float[pyarrow] with float64
    s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype="float[pyarrow]")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="float64")
    result = s.dot(df)
    expected_dtype = "float[pyarrow]"  # Should use the Arrow extension dtype
    assert str(result.dtype) == expected_dtype

def test_series_dot_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases for Series.dot."""
    
    # Empty series
    s_empty = pd.Series([], dtype="Float64")
    df_empty = pd.DataFrame([], dtype="Float64")
    result_empty = s_empty.dot(df_empty)
    assert len(result_empty) == 0
    
    # Single element
    s_single = pd.Series([1.0], dtype="Float64")
    df_single = pd.DataFrame([[1.0]], dtype="Float64")
    result_single = s_single.dot(df_single)
    assert result_single.iloc[0] == 1.0
    assert str(result_single.dtype) == "Float64"
    
    # NaN values
    s_nan = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan], dtype="Float64")
    df_nan = pd.DataFrame([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype="Float64")
    result_nan = s_nan.dot(df_nan)
    assert pd.isna(result_nan.iloc[0]) or pd.isna(result_nan.iloc[1])
    
    # Large values
    s_large = pd.Series([1e10, 2e10], dtype="Float64")
    df_large = pd.DataFrame([[1e10, 2e10], [3e10, 4e10]], dtype="Float64")
    result_large = s_large.dot(df_large)
    assert not pd.isna(result_large.iloc[0]) and not pd.isna(result_large.iloc[1])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_series_dot_nullable_dtypes()
    test_series_dot_arrow_dtypes()
    test_series_dot_mixed_dtypes()
    test_series_dot_edge_cases()
    print("All edge case tests passed!")</parameter>

In order for PPS sampling without replacement to be feasible, the selection probabilities must be less than 1, i.e.

$ \frac{n \cdot w_i}{\sum w_i}< 1$

For example, suppose you want to select 2 units with PPS without replacement from a sampling frame of 3 units with sizes 100, 1, and 1. There is no way to make the probability of selection of the first unit 100x the probability of selection of the other two units (since the max prob for the first unit is 1 and at least one of the other units must have prob >= .5).

Unfortunately, pandas df.sampling function doesn't throw an error in this case.

    print("\n1. Testing valid case...")

    print("\n2. Testing boundary case...")

    df2 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [1, 1, 1]})  # Equal weights, n=3, max_weight=1/3, 1/3*3=1
    try:
        result = df2.sample(n=3, weights=df2.w, replace=False)
        print("✓ Boundary case passed")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Boundary case failed: {e}")
    
    # Test 3: Invalid case - weights too large
    print("\n3. Testing invalid case...")
    df3 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [100, 1, 1]})

        print("✗ Invalid case should have failed")
    except ValueError as e:
        if "PPS sampling" in str(e):

        else:
            print(f"✗ Invalid case raised wrong error: {e}")
    
    # Test 4: With replacement should still work
    print("\n4. Testing with replacement...")
    df4 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [100, 1, 1]})
    try:
        result = df4.sample(n=2, weights=df4.w, replace=True)
        print("✓ With replacement case passed")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ With replacement case failed: {e}")
    
    # Test 5: Single element sampling
    print("\n5. Testing single element sampling...")
    df5 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [100, 1, 1]})
    try:
        result = df5.sample(n=1, weights=df5.w, replace=False)
        print("✓ Single element case passed")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Single element case failed: {e}")
    
    # Test 6: Zero weights
    print("\n6. Testing zero weights...")
    df6 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [0, 0, 0]})
    try:
        result = df6.sample(n=1, weights=df6.w, replace=False)
        print("✗ Zero weights case should have failed")
    except ValueError as e:
        if "sum to zero" in str(e):
            print("✓ Zero weights case correctly raised sum to zero error")
        else:
            print(f"✗ Zero weights case raised wrong error: {e}")
    
    # Test 7: Negative weights
    print("\n7. Testing negative weights...")
    df7 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [1, -1, 2]})
    try:
        result = df7.sample(n=1, weights=df7.w, replace=False)
        print("✗ Negative weights case should have failed")
    except ValueError as e:
        if "negative" in str(e):
            print("✓ Negative weights case correctly raised negative error")
        else:
            print(f"✗ Negative weights case raised wrong error: {e}")
    
    # Test 8: Large dataset with moderate weights
    print("\n8. Testing large dataset...")
    np.random.seed(42)
    large_weights = np.random.exponential(scale=1, size=1000)
    df8 = pd.DataFrame({'w': large_weights})
    try:
        result = df8.sample(n=100, weights=df8.w, replace=False)
        print("✓ Large dataset case passed")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Large dataset case failed: {e}")
    
    # Test 9: Fraction sampling
    print("\n9. Testing fraction sampling...")
    df9 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [100, 1, 1, 1, 1]})
    try:
        result = df9.sample(frac=0.4, weights=df9.w, replace=False)  # 2 out of 5
        print("✓ Fraction sampling case passed")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Fraction sampling case failed: {e}")
    
    # Test 10: Fraction sampling that would be invalid
    print("\n10. Testing invalid fraction sampling...")
    df10 = pd.DataFrame({'w': [100, 1, 1]})
    try:
        result = df10.sample(frac=0.8, weights=df10.w, replace=False)  # 2.4 out of 3
        print("✗ Invalid fraction case should have failed")
    except ValueError as e:
        if "PPS sampling" in str(e):
            print("✓ Invalid fraction case correctly raised PPS error")
        else:
            print(f"✗ Invalid fraction case raised wrong error: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":

ENH: support new-style float_format string in to_csv
### Feature Type

- [X] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

**The `float_format` parameter in `pd.DataFrame.to_csv` doesn't support modern (i.e. since Python 2.6) format strings yet.**

The documentation says about the `float_format` parameter:

> **float_format : float_formatstr, Callable, default None** Format string for floating
> point numbers. If a Callable is given, it takes precedence over other
> numeric formatting parameters, like decimal.

The word "format string" apparently means an [old-style %-format string](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#old-string-formatting) like `"%.6f"`. However, the Python docs tend to use that word for a [modern format string](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#the-string-format-method) like `"{:.6f}"`.

```
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([0.1, 0.2])

for float_format in ["%.6f", "{:.6f}".format, "{:.6f}"]:
    print(float_format, ":\n", df.to_csv(float_format=float_format))
```

Out:
```
%.6f :
 ,0
0,0.100000
1,0.200000

<built-in method format of str object at 0x7f62be4e01f0> :
 ,0
0,0.100000
1,0.200000

{:.6f} :
 ,0
0,{:.6f}
1,{:.6f}
```

### Feature Description

pseudo code:
```
class DataFrame:
...
    def to_csv(..., float_format, ...):
        if isinstance(float_format, str):
            if "%" in float_format:
                float_format = lambda x: float_format % x
            else:
                float_format = float_format.format
        ...
        out = float_format(value)
        ...
```

### Alternative Solutions

#### Workaround
```
df.to_csv(float_format="{.6f}".format)
```

#### Documentation change

Document that:

- only old-style % format strings are supported.
- one can pass in a string's format method (e.g. `float_format = "{:.6f}".format`) if one wants to use a modern format string.

### Additional Context

If this feature is implemented and used, one could get a minor speed-up in Python 3.10 compared to using %-strings (The same speedup is accessible by using the workaround described above.):

```
from timeit import timeit

num = 0.1

print("%:", timeit('"%.6f" % 0.1'))
print("format:", timeit('"{:.6f}".format(0.1)'))

setup = '''
from numpy.random import rand
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(rand(1000, 1000))
'''

print("% to_csv:", timeit(
    'df.to_csv(float_format="%.6f")', setup=setup, number=10))
print("format to_csv:", timeit(
    'df.to_csv(float_format="{:.6f}".format)', setup=setup, number=10))
```

Output:
```
%: 0.10213060600017343
format: 0.10648653099997318
% to_csv: 7.168424273999335
format to_csv: 5.367143424999995
```

import pandas as pd

import pytest

def test_none_column_sorting():
    """Test various edge cases for sorting with None column names"""
    
    # Test 1: Basic None column sorting
    print("Test 1: Basic None column sorting")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    result = df.sort_values(None)
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ Basic None column sorting works")
    
    # Test 2: Descending sort with None
    print("Test 2: Descending sort with None")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    result = df.sort_values(None, ascending=False)
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[3, 4], [1, 2]], columns=['C1', None], index=[1, 0])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ Descending sort with None works")
    
    # Test 3: Multiple None columns (should raise error for ambiguity)
    print("Test 3: Multiple None columns")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], columns=[None, 'C2', None])
    try:
        result = df.sort_values(None)
        print("✗ Should have raised error for ambiguous None")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✓ Correctly raised error: {type(e).__name__}")
    
    # Test 4: Sort by multiple columns including None
    print("Test 4: Multiple columns including None")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], columns=['C1', None, 'C3'])
    result = df.sort_values([None, 'C1'])
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], columns=['C1', None, 'C3'])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ Multiple columns including None works")
    
    # Test 5: None column with NaN values
    print("Test 5: None column with NaN values")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, np.nan], [5, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    result = df.sort_values(None)
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2.0], [5, 4.0], [3, np.nan]], 
                           columns=['C1', None], index=[0, 2, 1])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ None column with NaN values works")
    
    # Test 6: Empty DataFrame with None column
    print("Test 6: Empty DataFrame with None column")
    df = pd.DataFrame(columns=[None])
    result = df.sort_values(None)
    expected = pd.DataFrame(columns=[None])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ Empty DataFrame with None column works")
    
    # Test 7: Series with None name
    print("Test 7: Series with None name")
    s = pd.Series([3, 1, 2], name=None)
    result = s.sort_values()
    expected = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], name=None, index=[1, 2, 0])
    pd.testing.assert_series_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ Series with None name works")
    
    # Test 8: MultiIndex with None level names
    print("Test 8: MultiIndex with None level names")
    arrays = [['A', 'A', 'B', 'B'], [1, 2, 1, 2]]
    index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=[None, 'level'])
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6], [7, 8]], 
                     columns=['C1', 'C2'], index=index)
    result = df.sort_values('C1')
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6], [7, 8]], 
                           columns=['C1', 'C2'], index=index)
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ MultiIndex with None level names works")
    
    # Test 9: Verify None as index name doesn't interfere
    print("Test 9: None as index name")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    df.index.name = None
    result = df.sort_values(None)
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', None])
    expected.index.name = None
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ None as index name doesn't interfere")
    
    # Test 10: Verify other None-like values still work
    print("Test 10: String 'None' column")
    df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', 'None'])
    result = df.sort_values('None')
    expected = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=['C1', 'None'])
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
    print("✓ String 'None' column works")
    
    print("\n🎉 All edge case tests passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_none_column_sorting()</parameter>

from datetime import datetime
from pandas.tseries.holiday import Holiday, AbstractHolidayCalendar
from pandas import DateOffset
from dateutil.relativedelta import MO

# Create the UK Spring Bank Holiday rule as described in the issue
uk_spring_holiday = Holiday(
    "UK Spring Bank Holiday", 
    month=5, 
    day=31, 
    offset=DateOffset(weekday=MO(-1))
)

# Check what dates this generates for 2022
print("Original UK Spring Bank Holiday dates for 2022:")
dates = uk_spring_holiday.dates(datetime(2022, 1, 1), datetime(2022, 12, 31))
print(dates)

# The issue: we want to exclude May 30, 2022 (original date) 
# and instead have June 2, 2022 as the holiday
# But there's no built-in way to exclude specific dates

# Current workaround as mentioned in the issue
rules = [
    Holiday("UK Spring Hol pre Jubilee", end_date=datetime(2022, 5, 1), month=5, day=31, offset=DateOffset(weekday=MO(-1))),
    Holiday("Queen Jubilee Thu", year=2022, month=6, day=2),
    Holiday("Queen Jubilee Fri", year=2022, month=6, day=3),
    Holiday("UK Spring Hol post Jubilee", start_date=datetime(2022, 7, 1), month=5, day=31, offset=DateOffset(weekday=MO(-1))),
]

class UKCalendar(AbstractHolidayCalendar):
    rules = rules

calendar = UKCalendar()
holidays = calendar.holidays(datetime(2022, 1, 1), datetime(2022, 12, 31))
print("\nCurrent workaround holidays:")
print(holidays)

try:

print("Testing exclude_dates functionality...")

    month=5, 
    day=31, 
    offset=DateOffset(weekday=MO(-1)),
    exclude_dates=[datetime(2022, 5, 30)]
)

)

print(f"2023-12-25 excluded: {datetime(2023, 12, 25) not in dates}")

normal_holiday = Holiday(
    "Normal Holiday",
    month=7,
    day=4
)

print("\nTest 3: Normal holiday without exclude_dates")
dates = normal_holiday.dates(datetime(2022, 1, 1), datetime(2022, 12, 31))
print(f"Dates: {dates}")

# Test 4: Empty exclude_dates
empty_exclude_holiday = Holiday(
    "Empty Exclude Holiday",
    month=7,
    day=4,
    exclude_dates=[]
)

print("\nTest 4: Holiday with empty exclude_dates")

print(f"Dates: {dates}")

# Test 5: Integration with AbstractHolidayCalendar
class TestCalendar(AbstractHolidayCalendar):
    rules = [
        Holiday(

            month=5, 
            day=31, 
            offset=DateOffset(weekday=MO(-1)),

    ]

```max_len_string_array(ensure_object(encoded._values))```
by
```max_len_string_array(ensure_object(self.data[col]._values))```

2. But encoded length > 2045 (due to multi-byte characters like '§')

"""
Edge case tests for the PyTables error message fix.
"""

import sys
import tempfile
import os
import subprocess

def test_error_message_consistency():
    """Test that error messages are consistent across different HDF5 operations."""
    
    print("=== Testing Error Message Consistency ===")
    
    # Test different HDF5 operations that should all give the same error
    operations = [
        ("HDFStore", """
import pandas as pd
try:
    store = pd.HDFStore("test.h5")
except ImportError as e:
    print(str(e))
"""),
        ("to_hdf", """
import pandas as pd
import tempfile
import os
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3]})
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.h5', delete=False) as tmp:
    tmp_path = tmp.name
try:
    df.to_hdf(tmp_path, key='test')
except ImportError as e:
    print(str(e))
finally:
    try:
        os.unlink(tmp_path)
    except:
        pass
""")
    ]
    
    for operation_name, test_script in operations:
        print(f"\nTesting {operation_name}...")
        
        try:
            result = subprocess.run([
                sys.executable, '-c', test_script
            ], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
            
            error_msg = result.stderr.strip() or result.stdout.strip()
            print(f"  Error: {error_msg}")
            
            # Check that the error message suggests 'tables' not 'pytables'
            if "tables" in error_msg and "pytables" not in error_msg:
                print(f"  ✓ {operation_name}: Error message correctly suggests 'tables'")
            else:
                print(f"  ✗ {operation_name}: Error message issue persists")
                return False
                
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            print(f"  ✗ {operation_name}: Test timed out")
            return False
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  ✗ {operation_name}: Unexpected error: {e}")
            return False
    
    return True

def test_import_optional_dependency_directly():
    """Test the import_optional_dependency function directly."""
    
    print("\n=== Testing import_optional_dependency Directly ===")
    
    test_script = """
from pandas.compat._optional import import_optional_dependency
try:
    tables = import_optional_dependency("tables")
except ImportError as e:
    print(str(e))
"""
    
    try:
        result = subprocess.run([
            sys.executable, '-c', test_script
        ], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
        
        error_msg = result.stderr.strip() or result.stdout.strip()
        print(f"Direct import error: {error_msg}")
        
        if "tables" in error_msg and "pytables" not in error_msg:
            print("✓ Direct import: Error message correctly suggests 'tables'")
            return True
        else:
            print("✗ Direct import: Error message issue persists")
            return False
            
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Direct import test failed: {e}")
        return False

def test_version_requirements():
    """Test that version requirements are still checked correctly."""
    
    print("\n=== Testing Version Requirements ===")
    
    test_script = """
from pandas.compat._optional import import_optional_dependency
try:
    tables = import_optional_dependency("tables", min_version="999.0.0")
except ImportError as e:
    print(str(e))
"""
    
    try:
        result = subprocess.run([
            sys.executable, '-c', test_script
        ], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
        
        error_msg = result.stderr.strip() or result.stdout.strip()
        print(f"Version check error: {error_msg}")
        
        # Should mention version requirement, not package name issue
        if "tables" in error_msg and "999.0.0" in error_msg:
            print("✓ Version requirements are correctly checked")
            return True
        else:
            print("✗ Version requirements may not be working")
            print(f"  Got: {error_msg}")
            return False
            
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Version check test failed: {e}")
        return False

def test_other_packages_unchanged():
    """Test that other packages in INSTALL_MAPPING are unaffected."""
    
    print("\n=== Testing Other Packages Unchanged ===")
    
    # Test a few other packages that have different import vs install names
    test_cases = [
        ("bs4", "beautifulsoup4"),
        ("sqlalchemy", "SQLAlchemy"),
    ]
    
    for import_name, expected_install_name in test_cases:
        test_script = f"""
from pandas.compat._optional import import_optional_dependency
try:

except ImportError as e:

        except Exception as e:
            print(f"✗ {import_name}: Test failed: {e}")
            return False

    expected = Index([False, True, False], name="test_bool")
    print(f"Expected: {expected} (type: {type(expected)})")

API: inconsistency in casting back to its EA dtype (try_cast_to_ea)
With the current logic we have in `try_cast_to_ea`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/a72eef5a86979232337149961d2122f0b555c876/pandas/core/arrays/base.py#L49-L54

it's easy to get inconsistencies, and it depends critically on what `_from_sequence` accepts as valid scalar. 

For example, we now have this

```
>>> s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2], dtype="Int64") 
>>> s.combine(0, lambda x, y: x == y)      
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
```

However, if the IntegerArray constructor gets changed slightly to be more willing to accept all kinds of boolean like values (see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/31104 for a current inconsistency on this aspect, and this is what happens in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/30282), you can get:

```
>>> s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2], dtype="Int64")  
>>> s.combine(0, lambda x, y: x == y)       
0    1
1    0
2    0
dtype: Int64
```

So how "forgiving" the EA constructor is, will determine the output type. 

Here the example is with `combine`, but the `try_cast_to_ea` function is also used in a part of `groupby`.

```python
import pandas as pd
```

def test_combine_issue():
    """Test the combine issue mentioned in the GitHub issue."""
    print("Testing combine issue...")
    
    # Create a Series with Int64 dtype
    s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2], dtype="Int64")
    print(f"Original series: {s}")
    print(f"Original dtype: {s.dtype}")
    
    # Use combine with a lambda that returns boolean
    result = s.combine(0, lambda x, y: x == y)
    print(f"Result of combine: {result}")
    print(f"Result dtype: {result.dtype}")
    
    # Expected: boolean dtype, but we might get Int64 due to the issue
    expected_dtype = "bool"
    actual_dtype = str(result.dtype)
    
    print(f"Expected dtype: {expected_dtype}")
    print(f"Actual dtype: {actual_dtype}")
    
    if actual_dtype == expected_dtype:
        print("✓ PASS: Correct dtype returned")
    else:
        print("✗ FAIL: Incorrect dtype returned - this demonstrates the issue")
    
    return result.dtype == expected_dtype

def test_groupby_agg_issue():
    """Test the groupby agg issue with pyarrow timestamp."""
    try:
        import pyarrow as pa
        
        print("\nTesting groupby agg issue with pyarrow timestamp...")
        
        dtype = pd.ArrowDtype(pa.timestamp(unit="ns", tz="UTC"))
        dti = pd.date_range("2012-01-01", periods=4, tz="UTC").astype(dtype)
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [0, 0, 1, 1], "b": dti})
        
        gb = df.groupby("a")
        
        result = gb["b"].agg(lambda x: x.iloc[0].year)
        expected = pd.Series([2012, 2012], name="b")
        expected.index.name = "a"
        
        print(f"Result: {result}")
        print(f"Expected: {expected}")
        print(f"Result dtype: {result.dtype}")
        print(f"Expected dtype: {expected.dtype}")
        
        try:
            pd.testing.assert_series_equal(result, expected)
            print("✓ PASS: Series are equal")
            return True
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"✗ FAIL: {e}")
            return False
            
    except ImportError:
        print("PyArrow not available, skipping groupby test")
        return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    combine_pass = test_combine_issue()
    groupby_pass = test_groupby_agg_issue()
    
    if combine_pass and groupby_pass:
        print("\n✓ All tests passed")
    else:
        print("\n✗ Some tests failed - issue reproduced")</parameter>

def test_period_index_normalize_caching():
    """Test to reproduce the PeriodIndex normalize caching issue."""

    # Test case 1: First call with normalize=True
    print("\n=== Test Case 1: First call with normalize=True ===")

    print("\n=== Test Case 2: Second call with normalize=False ===")
    pi2 = pd.PeriodIndex(['19910905'], freq=pd.offsets.YearEnd(normalize=False))
    print(f"pi2.freq.normalize = {pi2.freq.normalize}")
    
    # This should be False, but due to caching it will be True
    expected = False
    actual = pi2.freq.normalize
    
    if actual == expected:
        print("✅ PASS: normalize=False correctly returned False")
        return True
    else:
        print(f"❌ FAIL: Expected {expected}, got {actual}")
        print("This demonstrates the caching issue described in the bug report")
        return False

def test_period_index_normalize_caching_reverse():
    """Test the reverse case - starting with normalize=False."""

    # Test case 2: Second call with normalize=True (should be True, but cached as False)
    print("\n=== Test Case 2: Second call with normalize=True ===")
    pi2 = pd.PeriodIndex(['19910905'], freq=pd.offsets.YearEnd(normalize=True))
    print(f"pi2.freq.normalize = {pi2.freq.normalize}")

    expected = True
    actual = pi2.freq.normalize
    
    if actual == expected:
        print("✅ PASS: normalize=True correctly returned True")
        return True
    else:
        print(f"❌ FAIL: Expected {expected}, got {actual}")
        print("This demonstrates the caching issue described in the bug report")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Test the original issue
    result1 = test_period_index_normalize_caching()
    result2 = test_period_index_normalize_caching_reverse()
    
    if not result1 or not result2:
        print("\n🔍 Issue reproduced! The normalize option is being cached per process.")

    else:
        print("\n✅ No issue found - normalize values are working correctly")

import pandas as pd
import warnings

def test_issue():
    """Test the issue described in the GitHub issue."""
    print("=" * 60)
    print("Reproducing the issue...")
    
    # Create the test data as described in the issue
    s = pd.Series(["2020-05-31 08:00:00", "2000-12-31 04:00:05", "1800-03-14 07:30:20"], dtype='datetime64[ms]')
    
    print("Original Series:")
    print(s)
    print(f"dtype: {s.dtype}")
    
    print("\nTesting dt.round('U') (microseconds)...")
    
    # Capture warnings
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        result = s.dt.round('U')
        
        if w:
            print("Warnings captured:")
            for warning in w:
                print(f"  {warning.category.__name__}: {warning.message}")
        else:
            print("No warnings captured.")
    
    print("Result:")
    print(result)
    
    # Check if the issue is present
    expected = s  # According to issue description, should be no-op
    print("\nExpected:")
    print(expected)
    
    print("\nAre they equal?", result.equals(expected))
    
    if not result.equals(expected):
        print("ISSUE PRESENT: Results don't match expected values")
        return False
    else:
        print("ISSUE FIXED: Results match expected values")
        return True

def test_edge_cases():
    """Test various edge cases related to rounding with different units."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Testing edge cases...")
    
    # Test different datetime resolutions
    test_cases = [
        ("datetime64[ns]", ["2020-05-31 08:00:00.123456789", "2000-12-31 04:00:05.987654321"]),
        ("datetime64[us]", ["2020-05-31 08:00:00.123456", "2000-12-31 04:00:05.987654"]),
        ("datetime64[ms]", ["2020-05-31 08:00:00.123", "2000-12-31 04:00:05.987"]),
        ("datetime64[s]", ["2020-05-31 08:00:00", "2000-12-31 04:00:05"]),
    ]
    
    units_to_test = ['ns', 'us', 'ms', 's', 'h', 'D']
    
    for dtype, dates in test_cases:
        print(f"\nTesting with {dtype}:")
        s = pd.Series(dates, dtype=dtype)
        print(f"  Original: {s}")
        
        for unit in units_to_test:
            try:
                with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
                    warnings.simplefilter("always")
                    result = s.dt.round(unit)
                    
                    if w:
                        print(f"    round('{unit}') -> WARNING: {w[0].message}")
                    else:
                        print(f"    round('{unit}') -> OK")
                        
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"    round('{unit}') -> ERROR: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_issue()
    test_edge_cases()</parameter>

import numpy as np

def test_empty_dataframe_join_preserves_index():
    """Test that join preserves index type for empty dataframes"""
    
    # Test 1: Object dtype index
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="object"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "object", f"Expected object dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    print("✓ Test 1 passed: Object dtype index preserved")
    
    # Test 2: String dtype index
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="string"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "string", f"Expected string dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    print("✓ Test 2 passed: String dtype index preserved")
    
    # Test 3: Int64 index
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="int64"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "int64", f"Expected int64 dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    print("✓ Test 3 passed: Int64 dtype index preserved")
    
    # Test 4: Float64 index
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="float64"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "float64", f"Expected float64 dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    print("✓ Test 4 passed: Float64 dtype index preserved")
    
    # Test 5: DatetimeIndex
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.DatetimeIndex([]))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), f"Expected DatetimeIndex, got {type(result.index)}"
    print("✓ Test 5 passed: DatetimeIndex preserved")
    
    # Test 6: MultiIndex
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([], names=['A', 'B']))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.MultiIndex), f"Expected MultiIndex, got {type(result.index)}"
    print("✓ Test 6 passed: MultiIndex preserved")
    
    # Test 7: Named index
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="object", name="my_index"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "object", f"Expected object dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    assert result.index.name == "my_index", f"Expected name 'my_index', got {result.index.name}"
    print("✓ Test 7 passed: Named index preserved")
    
    # Test 8: Different join types
    foo = pd.DataFrame([], index=pd.Index([], dtype="object"))
    bar = foo.copy()
    
    for how in ['left', 'right', 'outer', 'inner']:
        result = foo.join(bar, how=how)
        assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index for {how}, got {type(result.index)}"
        assert result.index.dtype == "object", f"Expected object dtype for {how}, got {result.index.dtype}"
    print("✓ Test 8 passed: All join types preserve index")
    
    # Test 9: Non-empty dataframes (regression test)
    foo = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2]}, index=pd.Index(['a', 'b'], dtype="object"))
    bar = pd.DataFrame({'B': [3, 4]}, index=pd.Index(['a', 'b'], dtype="object"))
    result = foo.join(bar)
    assert isinstance(result.index, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(result.index)}"
    assert result.index.dtype == "object", f"Expected object dtype, got {result.index.dtype}"
    assert list(result.index) == ['a', 'b'], f"Expected ['a', 'b'], got {list(result.index)}"
    print("✓ Test 9 passed: Non-empty dataframes work correctly")
    
    print("\nAll edge case tests passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":

"""Script to reproduce the issue described in the GitHub issue."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

print("Testing quantile with boolean dtypes...")

# Test case 1: Series.quantile with bool dtype
print("\n=== Test case 1: Series.quantile with bool dtype ===")
arr = np.random.randn(1000) < 0
ser = pd.Series(arr)

    result = ser.quantile(0.5)

except Exception as e:
    print(f"Series.quantile(0.5) raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

# Test case 2: GroupBy.quantile with bool dtype

    result = gb.quantile(0.5)
    print(f"GroupBy.quantile(0.5) = {result}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"GroupBy.quantile(0.5) raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

# Test case 3: Series.quantile with nullable boolean dtype
print("\n=== Test case 3: Series.quantile with nullable boolean dtype ===")
arr_nullable = pd.array(np.random.randn(1000) < 0, dtype="boolean")
ser_nullable = pd.Series(arr_nullable)
print(f"Series dtype: {ser_nullable.dtype}")

try:
    result = ser_nullable.quantile(0.5)
    print(f"Series.quantile(0.5) = {result}")

# Test case 4: GroupBy.quantile with nullable boolean dtype

except Exception as e:

# Summary

"""
Script to reproduce the issue described in the GitHub issue.
The issue is that ExtensionArrays (EA) don't have ffill/bfill methods
like NDFrame objects do.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pandas.core.arrays import IntegerArray

def test_extension_array_missing_ffill_bfill():
    """Test that ExtensionArrays are missing ffill/bfill methods."""
    
    # Create an IntegerArray with NaN values
    data = [1, 2, None, 4, None, 6]
    arr = IntegerArray._from_sequence(data)
    
    print("Original array:", arr)
    print("Array type:", type(arr))
    
    # Test if ffill method exists
    try:
        result = arr.ffill()
        print("ffill() result:", result)
    except AttributeError as e:
        print("ERROR: ffill() method not found on ExtensionArray:", e)
    
    # Test if bfill method exists
    try:
        result = arr.bfill()
        print("bfill() result:", result)
    except AttributeError as e:
        print("ERROR: bfill() method not found on ExtensionArray:", e)
    
    # Test fillna with method='ffill' which should work
    try:
        result = arr.fillna(method='ffill')
        print("fillna(method='ffill') result:", result)
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERROR with fillna(method='ffill'):", e)
    
    # Test fillna with method='bfill' which should work
    try:
        result = arr.fillna(method='bfill')
        print("fillna(method='bfill') result:", result)
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERROR with fillna(method='bfill'):", e)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_extension_array_missing_ffill_bfill()</parameter>
